text: A hash table stores key value pairs. A hash function turns the key into an index into an array. When two keys land on the same index, we have a collision, which we can handle with chaining or open addressing. Lookups are constant time on average, and we resize the table when the load factor gets high.

Big O notation describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size grows. It ignores constant factors and lower order dumps. So it lets us compare algorithms fairly. For example, binary search takes logarithmic time while a simple scan of a list takes linear time.

A database index is a data structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. It makes reads faster, but it uses extra storage and slows down writes. Because every insert and update, it must also update the index. So we index the columns that queries filter on most often.

When you type a URL into a browser, the browser first asks DNS to find the server address. Then it opens a TCP connection and does a TLS handshake. After that it sends an HTTP request, receives the response and finally renders the page. Caching can skip several of these steps.

A process has its own memory space while threads inside a process share memory. Switching between threads is cheaper than switching between processes but shared memory means threads can have race conditions. So we need locks and processes gives better isolation when one of them crashes.
